body.text: Route diversity on paper is not the same as operational redundancy on the ground—India needs a trade continuity exercise to test which IMEC alternatives can actually work under pressure
This is part of the essay series: Sagarmanthan Edit 2026.

The India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) poses New Delhi with an economic and strategic question: can more diversified connectivity preserve India’s room for manoeuvre when established trade routes are disrupted?

Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea exposed the costs of relying on a limited number of maritime passages. International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates indicate that trade volumes through the Suez Canal fell by 50 percent year-on-year during the first two months of 2024. The disruption also drove up transport costs: according to the World Bank, freight rates from Shanghai to Rotterdam and Genoa were, on average, 230 percent higher by November 2024 than at the end of 2023. More fundamentally, however, the crisis showed that an alternative route may exist on a map but not be operational when it is most needed.

The key challenge for IMEC is therefore not simply route diversification but operational redundancy: the ability of an alternative port, railway, border crossing or digital route to absorb and move trade when the primary route fails.

The Red Sea crisis illustrates this distinction. As shipping companies diverted vessels away from the Suez Canal and around the Cape of Good Hope, trade volumes along the alternative route increased by an estimated 74 percent year-on-year during the first two months of 2024. Yet the diversion added 10 days or more to average delivery times, showing that an available alternative does not necessarily provide an equivalent service.

The same principle applies across IMEC: a second port has limited value if it lacks the capacity to accommodate diverted cargo; a railway cannot provide an effective alternative without the necessary transit approvals; and digital documentation will not accelerate trade if it is not recognised in the next jurisdiction. Resilience depends not on the number of assets associated with a corridor but on whether they can be activated together under pressure.

This distinction is particularly relevant to how India understands strategic autonomy. New Delhi has long sought to preserve room for manoeuvre through diversified partnerships rather than exclusive alignments. Strategic autonomy, however, should not be understood here as freedom from dependence. In an interconnected trading system, that is neither realistic nor necessary.
Multiple diplomatic partnerships do not automatically translate into multiple operational options if ostensibly different routes depend on the same chokepoint or vulnerable infrastructure.

The objective is instead to reduce concentrated vulnerability to particular routes, nodes or political arrangements. Multiple diplomatic partnerships do not automatically translate into multiple operational options if ostensibly different routes depend on the same chokepoint or vulnerable infrastructure.

The September 2023 IMEC memorandum envisaged maritime and rail links alongside electricity, digital connectivity and clean hydrogen infrastructure. The memorandum created a framework for future development, not an integrated corridor. This matters because commercial efficiency and crisis resilience are not the same. Under normal conditions, the cheapest route may remain the preferred route. An alternative involving additional transhipment, rail freight or border procedures may cost more.

Under the proposed IMEC model, for example, cargo travelling from India to Europe would be unloaded at a Gulf port, transferred to rail, moved across several jurisdictions and reloaded onto a vessel at a Mediterranean port. Each stage may add handling, storage, customs clearance and insurance costs that do not arise to the same extent along a direct maritime route through the Suez Canal. Yet an option that is commercially suboptimal under normal conditions may still have substantial strategic value if it preserves trade during a disruption.

Digital infrastructure demonstrates the same principle. Projects such as Blue–Raman can add route diversity between India, the Middle East and Europe, while networks such as the Pakistan and East Africa Connecting Europe (PEACE) cable show that digital infrastructure often cuts across geopolitical blocs. The relevant question is therefore not simply how many cables exist but whether routes are genuinely independent, access can be controlled, traffic can be switched and damaged infrastructure can be repaired quickly.

An operational alternative should meet four tests. Capacity: can the substitute port, railway or data route absorb the required flow? Authorisation: are customs approvals, transit rights and data-sharing arrangements already in place? Responsibility: who has authority to reroute cargo, and how does liability transfer between carriers and jurisdictions? Finance: who absorbs the additional costs, and does insurance coverage remain valid once the route changes?

Demand also matters. Maintaining spare port, rail, or warehousing capacity imposes costs. Without sufficient baseline cargo volumes, or mechanisms to compensate operators for maintaining contingency capacity, private companies may have little incentive to preserve assets whose primary value emerges during periods of disruption.

India could help address these gaps by proposing an IMEC stress test— a joint trade continuity exercise. Such an exercise need not wait for a fully operational IMEC: India and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have already developed bilateral frameworks for trade facilitation and logistics that could provide an initial testing ground.

Rather than waiting for the entire corridor to be completed, the first exercise could focus on IMEC's India–UAE maritime leg. Existing shipping services connect the Indian ports of Cochin and Mundra with Jebel Ali and Abu Dhabi, providing a physical route through which diversion procedures could be tested. This could be combined with the India–UAE Virtual Trade Corridor, which uses the Master Application for International Trade and Regulatory Interface (MAITRI) to connect customs and port authorities in the two countries. A pilot exercise could simulate the temporary unavailability of one port and measure whether cargo could be redirected through another, how quickly customs authorities could approve the diversion and whether digital documentation could be transferred without resubmission. The exercise could then expand to additional segments as new connections become operational.

The exercise would simulate the temporary loss of a port, border crossing, rail segment or digital system. Governments, customs agencies, port authorities, carriers, rail operators and insurers would then have to answer four practical questions: how much trade can be diverted, how long approvals take, who can activate the alternative and who bears the additional cost.

Performance should be measured rather than declared. Indicators could include substitute capacity, time to authorise rerouting, the share of documents accepted without resubmission, continuity of liability and insurance, additional cost per shipment and time required to restore normal service.

An initial stress test could simulate the temporary closure of Jebel Ali and the diversion of India–UAE cargo to Khalifa Port. The exercise would examine whether the alternative port could absorb the additional volume, how quickly customs and port authorities could approve the diversion, whether documentation submitted through the MAITRI platform would remain valid and how liability, insurance and additional costs would be allocated. The results should then inform concrete decisions. Capacity shortfalls could guide investment in port handling, storage and onward transport; approval delays could identify areas requiring regulatory harmonisation or mutual recognition of documents; and uncertainty over liability or financing could be addressed through pre-agreed contingency protocols.

A trade continuity exercise would not place the corridor under Indian control but would allow India to use its partnerships to convert route diversity into operational options—the form of strategic autonomy that matters during a disruption.

India should therefore propose a phased IMEC trade continuity exercise, beginning with the India–UAE maritime leg and expanding as additional segments become operational. New Delhi and its partners should establish a joint working group involving customs authorities, port operators, shipping companies, insurers and digital-platform providers; agree in advance on procedures for activating alternative routes; and repeat the exercise periodically as infrastructure and trade volumes change. A trade continuity exercise would not place the corridor under Indian control but would allow India to use its partnerships to convert route diversity into operational options—the form of strategic autonomy that matters during a disruption.
Lauren Dagan Amoss is a researcher and lecturer at Bar-Ilan University, specialising in India's foreign and security policy, India–Israel relations and the Indo-Pacific.
